patient.name: Siobhan Murphy
patient.complaint: Tiredness, bloating and pale loose stools for 8 months
background: No recent travel; drinks little alcohol

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with chronic diarrhoea plus a clue to the cause: autoimmune history and iron deficiency (coeliac), alcohol and epigastric pain (chronic pancreatitis), travel (Giardia), cholecystectomy (bile acid).

points: Loose, **pale, bulky stools** that are hard to flush.

steps.lead: Siobhan has **malabsorption**. The question is which level fails: mucosa (coeliac, Crohn's), pancreas, bile salts or infection.
Floating, foul, pale stools are **steatorrhoea**; tiredness and pallor hint at iron, B12 or folate deficiency.

steps.r: Young woman with **autoimmune** history, mouth ulcers and iron deficiency: **coeliac disease**, the commonest mucosal cause.

steps.title: Finding the cause of malabsorption
head: Cause
Clue in the stem
First test
rows: Autoimmune disease, mouth ulcers, iron deficiency

steps.lead: No travel, little alcohol and no gallbladder surgery: Siobhan's story points away from Giardia, pancreatitis and bile acid loss.

steps.text: Giardia gives **non-bloody**, greasy diarrhoea. Blood in the stool points away from malabsorption towards colitis.
Coeliac disease clusters with **other autoimmune disease**: type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease. Screen these patients.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?': anti-tTG IgA (or anti-endomysial) for coeliac, faecal elastase for pancreatic insufficiency, stool microscopy for Giardia. The gold standard for coeliac is duodenal biopsy.

steps.title: Siobhan's GP bloods
steps.text: Iron and folate deficiency with low albumin and calcium: proximal small bowel malabsorption.

visual.title: Siobhan's ferritin
visual.label: Siobhan 6
visual.caption: Iron deficiency in a young woman with diarrhoea: test for **coeliac disease**.

steps.lead: Siobhan's bloods show what she is short of; **faecal elastase**, faecal fat and stool microscopy check the other causes.

steps.q: Which test should come first for suspected coeliac disease?
steps.r: Serology first (**anti-tTG IgA** or anti-endomysial antibody) while she is still eating gluten; then biopsy to confirm.

steps.lead: Siobhan's tTG is strongly positive, so she is referred for **duodenal biopsy**, the gold standard.
If serology had been negative and the cause still unclear, **endoscopy with biopsy** would look for the underlying disease.

visual.title: Faecal elastase (pancreatic function)
visual.label: Comparison: alcohol-related pancreatitis 85
visual.caption: Siobhan's is normal; a low elastase points to **pancreatic** malabsorption.

steps.text: Coeliac serology and biopsy are falsely negative if the patient has **already stopped gluten**. Keep eating gluten until the tests are done.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' matched to the cause: lifelong gluten-free diet for coeliac, Creon for pancreatic insufficiency, cholestyramine for bile acid malabsorption, metronidazole for Giardia.

steps.q: Biopsy confirms coeliac disease. What is the definitive treatment?
steps.r: Coeliac disease is treated with a **lifelong gluten-free diet**; a short course will relapse.

steps.lead: Siobhan's cure is diet: gluten-free for life, with a dietitian's help.
Siobhan also gets **iron and folate** replacement; weight and bloods are rechecked to confirm she is responding.

visual.title: Siobhan on a gluten-free diet
visual.caption: Haemoglobin recovers as tTG falls: a falling tTG shows she is sticking to the diet.

steps.lead: For other causes the drug matches the defect: **metronidazole** for Giardia, **Creon** for pancreatic insufficiency, **cholestyramine** for bile acid loss.

steps.title: Treat the cause, then the deficiency
nodes: All: replace iron, B12, folate, fat-soluble vitamins; monitor

steps.lead: Siobhan's care follows NICE coeliac guidance; NICE chronic pancreatitis guidance covers enzyme replacement.

steps.text: Fat-soluble vitamins are **A, D, E and K**: steatorrhoea can cause night blindness, osteomalacia and a prolonged prothrombin time.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why coeliac causes iron deficiency, why pancreatitis gives steatorrhoea, why bile acid loss gives diarrhoea, why Giardia is non-bloody.

steps.lead: Gluten triggers an **autoimmune** response in Siobhan's duodenum, flattening the villi, which is why iron and folate are low.

steps.title: Coeliac disease: from gluten to anaemia
nodes: Less absorptive surface in proximal small bowel
Iron, folate, calcium, fat-soluble vitamins lost

steps.lead: Chronic pancreatitis fails at **digestion**: without lipase, fat is never broken down to be absorbed.
After cholecystectomy, bile acids reach the colon unabsorbed and irritate it, while fewer micelles mean fat malabsorption.

steps.q: Why is giardiasis diarrhoea usually non-bloody?
o: It adheres to the brush border without invading
steps.r: **Giardia** sticks to the duodenal/jejunal surface and disrupts the brush border but does not invade, so there is no bleeding.

steps.lead: Giardia sits on the mucosa rather than in it, giving watery, greasy, **non-bloody** stools.

steps.text: Iron and folate are absorbed **proximally** (duodenum, jejunum); B12 and bile acids are absorbed in the **terminal ileum**. Site of disease predicts the deficiency.

mcq.q: What is the most common mucosal cause of malabsorption?
What are pale, bulky, foul, floating stools called?
Which non-GI condition causes pancreatic malabsorption in young people?
What is the gold standard test for coeliac disease?
Which stool test assesses pancreatic exocrine function?
What is the treatment of bile acid malabsorption?

mcq.r: Given with meals in CF or chronic pancreatitis.

mcq.q: What does coeliac disease do to the small bowel?
mcq.r: Proximal small bowel loses surface area.

prompts.q: What are the main causes of malabsorption, grouped by mechanism?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: mucosa, pancreas, bile, infection.

points.p: Bile salt deficiency: liver disease, ileal disease, post-cholecystectomy
Chronic diarrhoea and steatorrhoea: pale, greasy, bulky, foul, hard to flush
Iron, B12, folate deficiency: pallor, anaemia
Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (A, D, E, K)

prompts.q: Give the clue that points to each cause: coeliac, chronic pancreatitis, Giardia, bile acid malabsorption.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one stem clue per cause.

points.p: Coeliac: autoimmune history, mouth ulcers, iron deficiency
Chronic pancreatitis or CF: epigastric pain, alcohol
Giardia: travel, infected water, flatulence, non-bloody
Bile acid: greenish diarrhoea after cholecystectomy

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: serology first, biopsy confirms, keep eating gluten.

points.p: Anti-tTG IgA or anti-endomysial antibodies first

prompts.q: Which tests investigate the other causes and the deficiencies?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one test per cause.

points.why: Low in chronic pancreatitis and CF.

points.p: Faecal fat for steatorrhoea; endoscopy and biopsy if still unclear

prompts.q: How is each cause of malabsorption treated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the drug fixes the defect.

prompts.q: What long-term support do all malabsorption patients need?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: treat the cause, replace, monitor.

points.why: Iron, folate, B12, A, D, E, K.

prompts.q: Why does coeliac disease cause malabsorption and which nutrients are lost?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: gliadin to villous atrophy.

points.p: Villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia in proximal small bowel
Less surface area: iron, folate, calcium, fat-soluble vitamins lost

prompts.q: Explain steatorrhoea in chronic pancreatitis, diarrhoea in bile acid malabsorption and why Giardia is non-bloody.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: digestion, micelles, no invasion.

points.p: Pancreatitis: less lipase, amylase, protease, so fat is not digested
points.why: A digestion failure, not just absorption.

points.p: Bile acids needed for micelles; unabsorbed bile acids irritate the colon
Giardia adheres to the brush border without invading

glossary.malabsorption: Failure to absorb nutrients from the gut.
glossary.steatorrhoea: Pale, bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools that float, from excess fat.
glossary.coeliac disease: Autoimmune reaction to gluten causing small bowel villous atrophy.
glossary.gluten: Protein in wheat, barley and rye that triggers coeliac disease.
glossary.gliadin: The part of gluten that triggers the immune response in coeliac disease.
glossary.villous atrophy: Flattening of the small bowel villi, reducing absorptive surface.
glossary.crypt hyperplasia: Lengthened, overactive crypts between villi, seen in coeliac disease.
glossary.villi: Finger-like projections of the small bowel lining that absorb nutrients.
glossary.brush border: Microvilli on enterocytes, carrying digestive enzymes.
glossary.tTG: Tissue transglutaminase; IgA antibodies against it are the first-line coeliac test.
glossary.anti-tTG IgA: Antibody blood test used to screen for coeliac disease.
glossary.anti-endomysial antibodies: Highly specific antibodies for coeliac disease.
glossary.duodenal biopsy: Tissue sample from the duodenum at endoscopy; gold standard for coeliac.
glossary.faecal elastase: Pancreatic enzyme measured in stool; low in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
glossary.faecal fat: Measure of fat in stool, confirming steatorrhoea.
glossary.chronic pancreatitis: Long-term pancreatic inflammation destroying exocrine and endocrine tissue.
glossary.pancreatic insufficiency: Too little pancreatic enzyme to digest food properly.
glossary.cystic fibrosis: Inherited CFTR defect causing thick secretions and pancreatic insufficiency.
glossary.Creon: Pancreatic enzyme replacement capsules taken with meals.
glossary.bile acid malabsorption: Unabsorbed bile acids reach the colon and cause watery diarrhoea.
glossary.bile acids: Detergent-like molecules from the liver that form micelles to absorb fat.
glossary.micelles: Tiny bile acid clusters carrying fat and fat-soluble vitamins to be absorbed.
glossary.cholestyramine: Bile acid sequestrant that binds bile acids in the gut.
glossary.Giardia lamblia: Protozoan parasite from untreated water causing malabsorption.
glossary.metronidazole: Antimicrobial for anaerobes and protozoa such as Giardia.
glossary.stool microscopy: Looking at stool under a microscope for parasites, cysts and cells.
glossary.fat-soluble vitamins: Vitamins A, D, E and K, absorbed with fat.
glossary.ferritin: Iron storage protein; low means iron deficiency.
glossary.folate: B vitamin absorbed in the proximal small bowel.
glossary.B12: Vitamin absorbed in the terminal ileum with intrinsic factor.
glossary.terminal ileum: The last part of the small bowel, absorbing B12 and bile acids.
glossary.albumin: Main blood protein; low in malnutrition and malabsorption.
glossary.Crohn's disease: Transmural inflammatory bowel disease that can cause malabsorption.
glossary.dermatitis herpetiformis: Itchy blistering rash on extensor surfaces linked to coeliac disease.
glossary.mouth ulcers: Painful sores in the mouth, seen in coeliac and Crohn's.
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume: size of red cells; low in iron deficiency.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman has had fatigue, bloating and loose stools for 6 months. She has type 1 diabetes and recurrent mouth ulcers. Her stools are pale and difficult to flush. She has not travelled abroad.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis in chronic diarrhoea: find the malabsorption, then the cause.
Steatorrhoea, fatigue, mouth ulcers, autoimmune disease, no travel.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Coeliac disease**.
**B. Coeliac disease.** Rule: autoimmune + steatorrhoea + mouth ulcers = coeliac.

technique.stem: A 54 year old man drinks 80 units of alcohol a week. He has recurrent epigastric pain radiating to his back and loose, pale, offensive stools that float. CT shows pancreatic calcification.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess the cause of his diarrhoea?

steps.x: Investigation: decide which organ is failing first.

clues: epigastric pain radiating to his back
steps.x: Chronic pancreatitis with steatorrhoea: exocrine insufficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Faecal elastase** measures pancreatic exocrine function.
**D. Faecal elastase.** Rule: pancreas question = faecal elastase.

technique.stem: A 45 year old woman has had urgent, watery, greenish diarrhoea since a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 6 months ago. Stool cultures, coeliac serology and colonoscopy are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management of a specific malabsorption cause.

clues: Stool cultures, coeliac serology and colonoscopy are normal
steps.x: Post-cholecystectomy diarrhoea with other causes excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bile acid malabsorption**: treat with **cholestyramine**.
**A. Cholestyramine.** Rule: after cholecystectomy = bile acid = cholestyramine.

technique.stem: A 50 year old man with chronic pancreatitis has pale, greasy stools that float. His faecal elastase is low.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his steatorrhoea?
o: Bile acid loss in the terminal ileum
Brush border disruption by a parasite

steps.x: Mechanism: which step of fat handling fails?
Exocrine pancreatic failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Less **lipase** means fat is not **digested**, so it cannot be absorbed.

elim: Bile acid malabsorption or ileal Crohn's.

steps.x: **C. Reduced pancreatic lipase secretion.** Rule: pancreas = digestion failure (lipase).

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has had tiredness, bloating and loose stools for 9 months. She has autoimmune hypothyroidism. She has lost 4 kg. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 106/66 mmHg. She looks pale.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Iron and folate deficiency (proximal absorption) with normal B12 and an autoimmune history points to coeliac disease. Crohn's of the ileum lowers B12.

steps.x: Diagnosis: chronic diarrhoea with deficiency.
Malabsorption with iron and folate deficiency and an autoimmune history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Coeliac disease**.

elim: Would usually give pain, RIF mass, raised CRP or B12 deficiency.
She is hypothyroid; no tremor or tachycardia.

steps.x: **A. Coeliac disease.** Rule: autoimmune + iron and folate deficiency + diarrhoea = coeliac.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has upper abdominal pain radiating to his back after meals and loose, pale, greasy stools. He drinks 90 units of alcohol a week and has recently developed diabetes. He has lost 8 kg. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his diarrhoea?
practice.e: Chronic pancreatitis destroys exocrine (steatorrhoea) and endocrine (diabetes) tissue. Coeliac disease does not cause back pain.

steps.x: Cause of chronic diarrhoea.
Alcohol, back-radiating pain, steatorrhoea and new diabetes (endocrine failure too).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic pancreatitis** with exocrine insufficiency.

elim: Weight loss and pain, but not steatorrhoea and diabetes.

steps.x: **B. Chronic pancreatitis.** Rule: alcohol + steatorrhoea + new diabetes = chronic pancreatitis.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man has had watery, foul-smelling, non-bloody diarrhoea, flatulence and bloating for 5 weeks. He returned from backpacking in South America, where he drank from mountain streams. He has lost 3 kg. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Giardia lamblia from untreated water causes non-bloody, malodorous diarrhoea with flatulence and malabsorption. Amoebiasis is bloody.

steps.x: Diagnosis in diarrhoea after travel.
Persistent non-bloody, malodorous diarrhoea and flatulence after untreated water.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Giardiasis**.

elim: Possible but travel and water point to infection.
Rare; months to years of residence in the tropics.

steps.x: **C. Giardiasis.** Rule: travel + stream water + flatulence + non-bloody = Giardia.

practice.stem: A 47 year old woman has had urgent, watery, greenish diarrhoea several times a day since her gallbladder was removed 4 months ago. She has no blood in her stools and no weight loss. Coeliac serology and stool cultures are negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Bile acid malabsorption classically follows cholecystectomy, giving greenish watery diarrhoea; it responds to cholestyramine.

steps.x: Diagnosis in diarrhoea after surgery.

clues: Coeliac serology and stool cultures are negative
steps.x: New diarrhoea after cholecystectomy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bile acid malabsorption**.

elim: A diagnosis of exclusion; the surgical trigger points to bile acid.
Older women on NSAIDs or PPIs; no surgical link.

steps.x: **A. Bile acid malabsorption.** Rule: post-cholecystectomy greenish diarrhoea = bile acid malabsorption.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman with a positive anti-tTG IgA has an upper GI endoscopy. Biopsies are taken from the second part of the duodenum.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on duodenal biopsy?
practice.e: Coeliac disease shows villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia in the proximal small bowel. Granulomas suggest Crohn's.

steps.x: Finding on biopsy: name the disease from the test result.
Positive tTG means coeliac disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia** (and intraepithelial lymphocytes).
**E. Villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia.** Rule: coeliac biopsy = villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia.

practice.stem: A 19 year old man with cystic fibrosis has bulky, pale, offensive stools that float. He is underweight. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. He has stopped taking some of his medicines.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his stools?
practice.e: Cystic fibrosis causes pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhoea and low faecal elastase; it is treated with Creon.

steps.x: Cause of steatorrhoea in a patient with a named disease.

clues: bulky, pale, offensive stools that float
stopped taking some of his medicines
steps.x: CF blocks pancreatic ducts; steatorrhoea after stopping medication (likely Creon).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency**.

elim: Possible in anyone, but CF plus stopped enzymes explains it.
Watery, bloating after milk; not steatorrhoea.

steps.x: **E. Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.** Rule: CF + steatorrhoea = pancreatic insufficiency.

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman has fatigue and loose stools. Blood tests show iron deficiency anaemia. She has not had any gastrointestinal tests and is eating a normal diet. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Coeliac disease is screened with anti-tTG IgA (or anti-endomysial antibody) while eating gluten; duodenal biopsy then confirms.

steps.x: Initial investigation: first step, not the gold standard.
Iron deficiency plus diarrhoea in a young woman: screen for coeliac.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anti-tTG IgA** serology first.

elim: Not first line in a young woman without bleeding or red flags.
Gold standard, done after positive serology.

steps.x: **A. Anti-tTG IgA.** Rule: suspect coeliac = serology (tTG IgA), then biopsy.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use has loose, pale, foul-smelling stools that are difficult to flush. He has lost weight despite a good appetite.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?
practice.e: Faecal elastase assesses pancreatic exocrine insufficiency from chronic pancreatitis.

steps.x: Investigation: which organ?
Steatorrhoea with alcohol: pancreatic insufficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Faecal elastase**.
**C. Faecal elastase.** Rule: alcohol + steatorrhoea = faecal elastase.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has coeliac disease confirmed on duodenal biopsy. He asks whether he can eat gluten again once he feels better.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Coeliac disease needs a strict lifelong gluten-free diet; any gluten continues the villous damage.

steps.x: Definitive management.
The answer must be about duration.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lifelong gluten-free diet**.

elim: Any gluten keeps the villi damaged.

steps.x: **B. Lifelong gluten-free diet.** Rule: coeliac = gluten-free for life.

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman has watery greenish diarrhoea since a cholecystectomy 1 year ago. Investigations for infection, coeliac disease and colitis are negative. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Cholestyramine, a bile acid sequestrant, treats bile acid malabsorption after cholecystectomy.

steps.x: Management of the identified cause.
Bile acid malabsorption.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cholestyramine** binds bile acids.
**A. Cholestyramine.** Rule: bile acid = cholestyramine.

practice.stem: A 21 year old woman with cystic fibrosis has steatorrhoea and poor weight gain. Faecal elastase is very low.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management for her steatorrhoea?
practice.e: CF pancreatic insufficiency is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon) with food, plus fat-soluble vitamins.

steps.x: Management of the identified mechanism.
Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Creon** (pancreatic enzymes) with meals and snacks.
**E. Pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals.** Rule: low elastase = Creon.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman has coeliac disease. She has iron deficiency anaemia, low folate and a normal vitamin B12.
practice.q: Which best explains this pattern of deficiency?
o: Villous atrophy in the proximal small bowel
practice.e: Coeliac villous atrophy mainly affects the duodenum and jejunum, where iron and folate are absorbed; B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum.

steps.x: Mechanism: match deficiency to site.
Iron and folate are absorbed proximally; B12 distally in the terminal ileum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Villous atrophy of the proximal small bowel** (duodenum and jejunum).

elim: Fat malabsorption, not iron and folate.

steps.x: **E. Villous atrophy in the proximal small bowel.** Rule: proximal = iron and folate; distal ileum = B12.
